title: Metaclasses: type, __new__, __init_subclass__, and Dynamic Class Generation

progressiveExplaining.eli5: In Python, everything is an object, including classes themselves. A normal class is a blueprint that creates objects. A metaclass is a 'super-blueprint' that creates the class itself. When Python reads `class MyClass:`, it calls the metaclass (usually `type`) to build the class object in memory.
progressiveExplaining.junior: In Python, `type` is both the default metaclass and a function. You can dynamically create a class using `type(name, bases, dict)`: `MyClass = type('MyClass', (object,), {'x': 10})`. To customize class creation, define a class inheriting from `type`: `class Meta(type): def __new__(cls, name, bases, dct): ...`. In modern Python (3.6+), you can often use `__init_subclass__` instead of full metaclasses for validating or registering subclasses.
progressiveExplaining.senior: Architecturally, Metaclasses intercept the three phases of class construction: (1) `__prepare__(metacls, name, bases)` returns the namespace dictionary (e.g. an `OrderedDict`), (2) `__new__(metacls, name, bases, namespace)` allocates the new `type` object, and (3) `__init__(cls, name, bases, namespace)` initializes the class before it is bound to the module namespace. Frameworks like Pydantic v1, Django ORM, and ABCs use metaclasses to inspect class attributes and build field registries.
progressiveExplaining.underTheHood: When executing a `class` statement, CPython resolves the metaclass via `PyType_CalculateMetaclass`. It invokes `metaclass.__prepare__()` to get the namespace. It executes the class body code within that namespace. Finally, it invokes `metaclass.__new__(metaclass, name, bases, namespace)` which calls `PyType_FromSpec` / `tp_new` to allocate the `PyTypeObject` struct in memory.

codeComparison.title: Heavy Metaclass vs Modern __init_subclass__ Hook
codeComparison.summary: Metaclasses add complexity and conflict risks; `__init_subclass__` provides simple subclass validation without metaclass overhead.

legacyOrBad.label: Complex Custom Metaclass
legacyOrBad.snippet: class ValidateMeta(type): def __new__(cls, name, bases, dct): ... // ❌ Metaclass conflict risk

modernOrGood.label: Modern __init_subclass__ Hook
modernOrGood.snippet: class BaseModel: def __init_subclass__(cls, **kwargs): ... // ✅ NEW: Clean, no metaclass conflicts

interviewGotchas.question: What causes a 'metaclass conflict' in Python, and how is it resolved?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Interviewers test your deep understanding of multiple inheritance and metaclass resolution.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: A metaclass conflict occurs when a class inherits from multiple base classes whose metaclasses are not subclasses of one another (e.g. Class A has `MetaA`, Class B has `MetaB`). When defining `class C(A, B):`, Python cannot determine which metaclass to use and throws `TypeError: metaclass conflict: the metaclass of a derived class must be a (non-strict) subclass of the metaclasses of all its bases`. The fix is to create a common derived metaclass: `class MetaC(MetaA, MetaB): pass`.
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: Prefer `__init_subclass__` or class decorators to avoid metaclass conflicts in public libraries.

interviewGotchas.question: What is the purpose of `__prepare__` in a metaclass?
interviewGotchas.contextIntro: Checks knowledge of the earliest stage of class definition in Python.
interviewGotchas.detailedAnswer: `__prepare__(metacls, name, bases)` is called **before the class body is executed**. It returns a mapping object (namespace) in which the class body's code will be executed. By default, it returns a standard `dict`. Before Python 3.6 (when dicts became insertion-ordered), metaclasses used `__prepare__` to return an `collections.OrderedDict` to preserve the exact declaration order of class attributes and fields (essential for ORMs).
interviewGotchas.trapWarning: `__prepare__` must be declared as a `@classmethod` or static method on the metaclass.
